title: Align Department Assessments with IB Criteria
summary: IB assessment alignment made simple: learn how rubrics, command terms, and calibration help you revise smarter and earn consistent marks across classes.
body_markdown:
If you have ever wondered why your friend got “great analysis” on an answer that earned you “too descriptive,” you have already met the hidden problem of inconsistent assessment.


In the **IB** , that inconsistency is not just annoying. It is expensive. It costs time, confidence, and revision energy because you start studying your teacher instead of studying the criteria.


The good news is that when a department aligns assessments with **IB** criteria, students feel it immediately: feedback becomes predictable, improvement becomes repeatable, and revision becomes calmer.


Same essay, three rubrics: the student experience


### What it means to align department assessments with IB criteria


Alignment is a simple promise: a “good response” stays good no matter which classroom you are in.


In practice, aligning departmental assessments with **IB** criteria means:


-


Your rubrics reflect the language of **IB** markbands (not a mystery “teacher rubric”).


-


Command terms are treated as skills, not vibes.


-


Two teachers can justify the same mark for the same reasons.


-


Feedback helps you improve the next task, not just explain the last one.


If you want the wider school perspective, this article connects the dots:[Aligning Departmental Assessments with IB Criteria](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/aligning-departmental-assessments-with-ib-criteria) .


### Quick student checklist: signs your IB assessments are aligned


From a student seat, alignment looks less like policy and more like a feeling: “I know what they want, and I can train it.”


Check for these signals:


-


Rubrics mention **IB** criteria strands and use familiar descriptors.


-


Teachers use the same command-term meanings (analyze vs evaluate vs discuss).


-


Grade decisions come with evidence (“This is Level 5 because…”) not just impressions.


-


Exemplars exist, and teachers refer to them.


-


Your improvement targets repeat across units (because the skills repeat in the **IB** ).


When those signals are missing, students often build revision habits around guesswork. That is the opposite of what the **IB** rewards.


### Why this matters for IB exam preparation (even if it feels “teacher stuff”)


The **IB** is not primarily testing whether you were present in class. It is testing whether you can *perform thinking* under constraints: select evidence, structure reasoning, communicate clearly, and make justified judgments.


When departmental assessments drift away from **IB** criteria, you can work hard and still train the wrong muscle.


### Consistency reduces stress and increases speed


Stress often comes from uncertainty, not difficulty.


If your department is aligned to **IB** criteria, you spend less time decoding preferences and more time practicing a stable set of skills. That stability is a revision advantage because you can iterate faster: attempt, receive feedback, adjust, repeat.


### Feedback becomes reusable across subjects


In a well-aligned **IB** program, “more analysis” means the same thing in History, English, and the sciences: make a claim, justify it, and show the implications.


This is why consistency in grading is not only “fair.” It is efficient.


Related reading:[How IB Teachers Can Maintain Consistency in Grading and Assessment](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-ib-teachers-can-maintain-consistency-in-grading-and-assessment) .


### Progress feels like a staircase, not a roulette wheel


Aligned **IB** assessments create a sense of progression. You can feel yourself becoming the kind of student who earns marks, because the criteria remain stable while the tasks get harder.


Misalignment feels like switching sports mid-season and still being surprised you are sore.


### Start with IB criteria, then design the assessment


A common reason departments drift is harmless: a teacher designs an engaging task first, then adds a rubric later.


But **IB** alignment works best in reverse:


-


Identify the **IB** criteria strands you are actually assessing.


-


Choose the command terms that will produce visible evidence.


-


Design the task so students cannot avoid those skills.


This matters for you because a criteria-first task is easier to revise for. You can practice the skill directly.


For MYP students, the same logic applies with criteria A--D:[Creating Rubrics Aligned with IB Criteria in the MYP](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/creating-rubrics-aligned-with-ib-criteria-in-the-myp) .


### Use shared templates that keep creativity but remove chaos


Departments sometimes hear “alignment” and imagine identical worksheets.


Good alignment is more like guardrails: you can still drive your own route, but everyone is using the same road rules.


A strong **IB** -aligned assessment template often includes:


-


Named criteria strands (explicit and visible)


-


Student-friendly success indicators tied to markbands


-


A short “what this looks like” section (mini exemplars or annotated snippets)


-


A reflection prompt linked to criteria (“Which strand held you back most, and what will you do next time?”)


Templates reduce the cognitive load of starting every task from scratch. When structure is familiar, your brain has more room for analysis and evaluation.


If you like the bigger idea of authenticity plus clarity, see:[Designing Assessments That Promote Authentic Understanding](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/designing-assessments-that-promote-authentic-understanding) .


### Calibration sessions: where IB alignment becomes real


You cannot align assessment through documents alone. Alignment lives in the moment two teachers look at the same paragraph and argue -- respectfully -- about what the markband language really means.


A simple calibration cycle looks like this:


-


Choose 3 anonymized samples (low, middle, high)


-


Everyone marks independently using **IB** criteria


-


Compare marks and (more importantly) reasons


-


Agree on which phrases best match the markband descriptors


-


Save those samples as department exemplars


This is not about forcing identical marks forever. It is about making differences principled instead of accidental.


Calibration session as “markband tasting”


Students benefit because calibrated marking produces calibrated feedback, and calibrated feedback produces targeted revision.


If you are curious about fairness and bias, this pairs well:[Reducing Bias and Increasing Fairness in Internal Grading](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/reducing-bias-and-increasing-fairness-in-internal-grading) .


### Horizontal and vertical alignment: the invisible engine of better revision


Students often experience alignment as “my grades make sense now.”


But there are two different types of alignment at work.


### Horizontal alignment (same course, same expectations)


Horizontal alignment means two classes in the same **IB** subject are graded similarly.


When that is strong:


-


You can compare feedback with friends without confusion.


-


Study groups become more effective because everyone is training the same skills.


-


A “Level 6” in one room is not a “Level 4” in another.


A practical example of school-wide standardization is here:[Using RevisionDojo to Standardize Internal Assessments Across Departments](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/using-revisiondojo-to-standardize-internal-assessments-across-departments) .


### Vertical alignment (skills build year to year)


Vertical alignment means the same criteria get more demanding over time.


In the **IB** , that is how vague labels become real skills. “Evaluation” becomes: compare interpretations, acknowledge limitations, and justify a conclusion with evidence.


To see how schools map this across programs, read:[Strengthening Vertical Curriculum Alignment Across IB Programs](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/strengthening-vertical-curriculum-alignment-across-ib-programs) .


Alignment feels like closing 19 arguing tabs


### How you can use alignment even if you cannot control it


You cannot run department meetings. But you can still revise like a student in an aligned **IB** program.


### Translate feedback into criteria language


When you get a comment like “too narrative” or “needs depth,” ask yourself:


-


Which criterion strand is this referring to?


-


Which command term did I fail to satisfy?


-


What would a one-markband improvement look like?


If you cannot answer, ask your teacher a criteria-based question: “Which criterion does this comment connect to?”


### Build a personal “criteria checklist”


Keep a living document of recurring feedback patterns. In the **IB** , the same errors repeat:


-


describing instead of analyzing


-


claims without evidence


-


evidence without explanation


-


evaluation without criteria


-


weak structure under time pressure


Your goal is to turn feedback into a reusable checklist that travels across tasks.


### Practice under stable conditions


Even in a misaligned environment, you can practice in a way that mirrors **IB** marking.


That is where RevisionDojo becomes useful as a consistent second opinion.

### Closing: In the IB, consistency is a study advantage


The quiet advantage of a great **IB** department is not strictness. It is consistency.


When departmental assessments align with **IB** criteria, you stop chasing hints and start building skills that transfer -- from unit to unit, teacher to teacher, and finally into the exam hall.


If you want your revision to feel more predictable, use tools that speak the same criteria language every time.
